title: Bicuspid aortic valve: greatest risk is early-onset aortic stenosis
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a routine check-up. The patient is feeling well, and he and his parents have no concerns. On physical examination, an ejection sound and soft systolic murmur are noted at the upper sternal border. Echocardiography is performed, and a representative image of the short-axis view at the aortic valve level shows an aortic valve with only two cusps (fusion of two of the three normal cusps). Based on the observed abnormal finding, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?

clues.text: an ejection sound and soft systolic murmur are noted at the upper sternal border
clues.note: An early systolic ejection sound (click) with a soft systolic murmur at the aortic area is the classic auscultatory sign of a bicuspid aortic valve.

clues.text: two cusps (fusion of two of the three normal cusps)
clues.note: A two-cusp aortic valve on the short-axis echo confirms a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), a common congenital anomaly (~1% of the population).

whatMatters: An ejection click + aortic systolic murmur with a two-cusp valve on echo = bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). Its MOST COMMON complication is EARLY-ONSET AORTIC STENOSIS from accelerated calcification of the abnormal valve (severe stenosis by ~age 40-50, vs >70 for a normal trileaflet valve). Answer B. (BAV also carries risk of aortic regurgitation and ascending aortic aneurysm/dissection.)
strategy: Identify BAV, then recall its natural history: turbulent flow across the abnormal valve accelerates calcification -> early aortic stenosis (the leading complication). Reject cryptogenic stroke (PFO), Eisenmenger (left-to-right shunt reversal), tet spells (tetralogy of Fallot), and sudden cardiac death (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) - none is the primary BAV risk.

eliminations.label: Cryptogenic stroke - patent foramen ovale
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale (PFO), a cause of cryptogenic stroke. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: BAV is a valve anomaly, not a right-to-left atrial shunt, and does not increase PFO prevalence. ✅ Correct if: young stroke with a PFO/atrial shunt.

eliminations.label: Eisenmenger syndrome - shunt reversal
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a long-standing left-to-right shunt (VSD/ASD/PDA) causing pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal with cyanosis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: BAV involves no left-to-right shunt, so it does not lead to Eisenmenger physiology. ✅ Correct if: unrepaired VSD/ASD/PDA with pulmonary hypertension.

eliminations.label: Episodic hypercyanotic spells - tetralogy of Fallot
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: 'tet spells' from dynamic right ventricular outflow obstruction in tetralogy of Fallot. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: BAV does not cause right-to-left shunting or cyanotic spells. ✅ Correct if: a cyanotic child with tetralogy of Fallot.

eliminations.label: Sudden cardiac death - hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: exertional sudden cardiac death classically linked to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in young athletes. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: BAV does not substantially raise sudden-death risk; its main sequela is progressive valve calcification/stenosis. ✅ Correct if: young athlete with HCM and dynamic outflow obstruction.

reasoning: Ejection click + aortic systolic murmur + two-cusp valve on echo = bicuspid aortic valve
Turbulent flow across the abnormal valve accelerates age-related valvular calcification
This causes EARLY-onset aortic stenosis (decades earlier than a normal trileaflet valve)
mechanism: A bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) results from fusion of two of the three normal aortic cusps, leaving two functional leaflets; it affects about 1% of the population, is more common in males, is often inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, and is associated with Turner syndrome. The abnormal geometry creates turbulent, high-shear flow that ACCELERATES age-related valvular calcification (a process akin to atherosclerosis), so significant aortic stenosis develops decades earlier than with a normal trileaflet valve - often by age 40-50, versus after 70 for a normal valve. Thus early-onset aortic stenosis is the most common complication and the correct 'greatest risk.' Less commonly, BAV disrupts valve closure to cause aortic regurgitation, and it is associated with ascending aortic aneurysm/dissection (from an intrinsic aortopathy). The auscultatory hallmark is an early ejection sound (click) with an aortic systolic murmur. The distractors belong to other congenital/structural lesions (PFO, left-to-right shunts, tetralogy of Fallot, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid CV > bicuspid aortic valve: ~1% population, ejection click; accelerated calcification -> early aortic stenosis (leading complication); also aortic regurgitation and ascending aortic aneurysm; Turner association.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Two-cusp valve on echo -> BAV; its natural history is early calcific aortic stenosis.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on bicuspid aortic valve, ejection click, valvular calcification, or aortopathy? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: PFO (cryptogenic stroke), left-to-right shunt (Eisenmenger), tetralogy (tet spells), and HCM (sudden death) are not BAV's principal risk.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the parasternal short-axis echo at the aortic valve: only TWO cusps open (a 'fish-mouth' orifice) instead of the normal Mercedes-Benz three-cusp pattern. Anchor: 'two cusps = bicuspid aortic valve -> early aortic stenosis.'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: bicuspid aortic valve -> early calcific aortic stenosis (± regurgitation, ascending aortic aneurysm); Turner association.

keywords.front: Ejection click + aortic murmur + two-cusp valve
Age of severe AS: BAV vs normal valve
Short-axis echo of normal aortic valve

memoryHook: Two cusps wear out fast: a bicuspid valve calcifies decades early, so aortic stenosis shows up in middle age instead of old age.
